I'm very conflicted on how I feel about Hammurabi's code. Pert of me thinks it's effective, the other - barbaric.

I feel like it's just humankind's first attempt to instill a sense of difference between ourselves and "the beasts". The notably barbaric parts put the safety of the individual above the productivity of the host civilization: if a very useful archer put out the eye of a handicapped farmhand, then the civilization lost an archer. I feel like the "other side" of that is taken too far in modern America, where being rich translates to, "the value of economy I do is greater than the loss to society of my crimes, therefore, you will unduly punish our society as a consequence of punishing me personally". That said, I certainly don't think "going back to basics" is the right remedy for that.

This isn't true at all. Humanity hasn't even always had the same morals regarding something as basic as murder. What constitutes murder? If I kill somebody who intended to kill me? Some would say yes. If I unintentionally stepped on an insect? Some would say yes. If I killed my daughter for being raped by a stranger? Some would say no.

And that's one of the most basic things that most of our cultures agree on. Take two steps out and say "Who is it appropriate to have sex with?" or "Who owns this object?" and you'll see just how different we all can be.

But the point stands that every culture has seen murder as wrong. There are exceptions, but this is the rule. Theft, rape, etc. are all seen as evil or bad for society. This was the point I was trying to make.
